newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Safrican abortion protesters clash with MPs.
newsitem.headline: Safrican abortion protesters clash with MPs.

text.p: Christian anti-abortion campaigners clashed with some members of South Africa's parliament on Monday over a proposed law which would allow abortion on demand.
Christian campaigners accused pro-choice legislators of ignoring majority opinion by promoting the will of an obdurate minority.
Politicians in the debate countered by urging anti-abortion groups at the public hearing to abandon confrontation and respect the new-found privilege of expressing their views in parliament.

"What disturbs me is that the churches have adopted a holier-than-thou pedestal," said legislator John Gogotya, a former lecturer in religion and a black member of the new-look National Party which installed apartheid and then scrapped it four decades later.

"...(We) have embarked on this to address a problem in South Africa which tends to mostly affect the already disadvantaged (black women). If we don't do anything, we will revert to the past," he said.
South African medical researchers say close to 50,000 women are hospitalised every year after botched illegal abortions. About 425 of them die each year.
But unofficial estimates say up to 120,000 women have illegal abortions ibn South Africa annually.
The law currently allows legal abortions in special circumstances such as pregnancy resulting from incest or rape or where the mother's life is endangered.
Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma, the first black woman in the job, has proposed a bill which would turn the country's abortion legislation to among the most liberal in the world.

It would allow women and underage girls to have abortions up until the 12th week of pregnancy on demand. They could also be allowed abortions for up to eight weeks more in cases involving physical or emotional risk, rape, sexual abuse or severe socio-economic circumstances.
Women's rights groups and the ruling African National Congress, which has a large majority in the two-chamber parliament, have thrown their weight behind relaxation of abortion laws.
But Christian lobbyists rejecting abortion under any circumstances have demanded a national referendum.
Barbara Muna, of the tiny African Christian Democratic Party, said the government wanted to ride rough-shod over the will of the majority of South Africans who she said were opposed to abortion.
"This country is meant to be a democracy, however when it comes to this issue it seems that the minority will decide," she said.
Members of parliament's lower house are scheduled to vote on the bill on October 29 and the senate on November 5 and will become law if passed by majorities in both houses.
